paragraphs: If you are willing to turn a vague idea into rules someone else can reproduce, and to test and revise them repeatedly, this is worth exploring. Saying this game is fun is not enough; you have to explain how goals, feedback, and choices interact.

First check whether the actual role covers systems, numbers, levels, or narrative, and what collaboration, scheduling, and tool requirements apply. Project pace and feedback shape the work experience, and one paper exercise does not prove that you can fit into a whole development team.

The systems and numbers direction focuses on rules, parameters, and balance; the level and narrative direction focuses on challenge, spatial progression, and story experience. Both are exploration directions within this occupation, with duties divided by team rather than forming a uniform promotion grade.

Complete the G20 offline key-and-door exercise on your own: calculate the route, verify the failure rules, then compare one mechanic change. No login, payment, or collection of real player data is needed; the work keeps the rules, the tests, and the reasons for changes.
Try this first: if you change the key and door, is the gameplay better?

Game design is not just proposing ideas. Only by writing goals, states, and action limits clearly can you discuss implementation with programmers and testers. G20 uses a single offline rule table to compare two routes and to separate can finish, uses fewer steps, and players prefer it. The last item needs experience evidence and cannot be derived from calculation.
The paper exercise only explores rule expression and testing habits; it does not prove commercial game design ability, position qualification, or player preference.

Observable signals are a willingness to state the initial state, action costs, and win or lose conditions, and to actively look for failure cases; after receiving a new requirement, revise the rules and tests rather than only the marketing description. You can explain the design rationale to different roles and admit that the experience is still unknown.

If you are only willing to propose ideas and not write rules, maintain documents, or accept test feedback, check your expectations first. Playing for a long time, ranking high, and being skilled with tools cannot on their own prove that you can design implementable gameplay; project and study time are arranged separately.

First complete G20 and keep the first version and the revised tests, then write out the questions that still need experience validation. Then, against three independent employer samples, choose the systems and numbers or the level and narrative direction, and check status, portfolio, and tool requirements.

O*NET15-1255.01 defines the core features of electronic games and the design of mechanics, story, and character background. Creating and maintaining design documents and collaborating with the production team are the work itself, not the duties of an actor or a visual director.

Design inputs include rules, resource limits, and test feedback, and action costs and failure handling must be consistent. In G20, each successful move costs 1 energy, and an illegal edge, insufficient energy, or a R0 door without a key all fail, with position, energy, and keys all unchanged. The rules and tests must keep these conditions together.

Systems and numbers design must state goals and states clearly in order to test rule relationships and parameters. In G20, the start is S, energy is 4, and keys are 0, and the map contains only four one-way edges, with reaching G a win that does not require keeping the key. Real balance still needs complete game conditions and experience validation.

Level and narrative design organizes challenge, tasks, story, and character background so that rules and experience progression work together. A good story outline still has to combine with gameplay, space, and the team's implementation conditions.

Deliverables may include rule specifications, configuration tables, prototypes, and test records, and changes must state their impact. The R1 change in G20 makes the door need no key and consume no key: the direct route can finish, the old key-collecting route is still legal but the key remains at the end, and the related routes and failure tests must be re-checked against the new version.

Communicate with programmers, artists, production, and testers to turn design requirements into confirmable implementation and acceptance conditions. Design advice does not automatically carry project scheduling, budget, or all technical decision rights.

O*NET lists tasks such as gameplay balance, prototyping, design review, and test planning. Tools serve these outputs, and no engine, programming language, or AI tool is treated as a uniform national qualification.

Continuous iteration must distinguish defects, rule changes, and experience hypotheses. Keeping versions, test inputs, and results helps explain the changes; specific user testing and data use follow the team's arrangements.

The following two work chains are editorially organized from O*NET tasks and recruitment directions and are not a uniform division of labor across all teams. The shared output is clear design rationale, implementable specifications, and a record of changes after testing.
Systems and numbers gameplay design
Define the goal → write rules and parameters → build a prototype → test boundaries → adjust balance → maintain the specification
Implementable and reviewable gameplay rules, configuration tables, and test records
Level and narrative design
Define the experience → arrange challenge and tasks → organize story progression → validate with a prototype → collect feedback → revise the level document
Level tasks, flow, character story, and their experience validation records
Shared preparation
Clear goals · rule expression · prototype validation · test feedback · cross-role collaboration · version maintenance
How do systems and numbers differ from level and narrative?

Systems and numbers focus on the relationships among mechanics, parameters, and progression; level and narrative focus on organizing challenge, tasks, story, and experience. Both need implementable documents and testing collaboration, and a job title does not guarantee exactly the same division of labor.
Core purpose
Build rules and feedback loops consistent with the goal.
Organize challenge and narrative so the experience unfolds progressively.
Design basis
Mechanic relationships, parameters, resource limits, and test results.
Spatial or task flow, story and characters, and gameplay limits.
Work process
Write states and parameters, validate with a prototype, and adjust balance.
Arrange tasks and challenges, validate progression, and revise the pacing.

Rule specifications, configuration tables, and test and version records.
Level flow, task descriptions, and story and character documents.
Responsibility boundaries
Explain the gameplay basis and acceptance conditions, with technical and project decisions following the team division.
Explain the experience goal and the connections, and do not replace implementation confirmation with a narrative idea.
Collaboration partners
Programmer, tester, artist, and production colleagues.
Programmer, artist, narrative, and tester colleagues.
Validation limits
Calculating a shorter route does not mean players will necessarily prefer it.
A complete story does not mean the level is already playable or that the experience meets the bar.
What does a design review judge first?

First confirm the goal, rules, implementation limits, and evidence. G20 can check states and routes and cannot replace real experience testing. The questions below are editorial self-checks, not a uniform hiring standard.
Are the win condition and initial state written clearly?
Are action costs and post-failure states consistent?
Which routes and tests does the change actually affect?
Is a shorter route necessarily more fun?
Not necessarily. Fewer steps is a rule calculation result, while fun and preference need a defined audience and experience evidence.
Has the prototype already proven a commercial outcome?
No. A prototype validates a specific hypothesis and cannot directly imply retention, revenue, or the preference of all players.
Can programmers and testers reproduce it from the document?

Collaborate｜implementation and version maintenance｜Work with programmers, artists, and testers to confirm the specification and the scope of change.
Section heading｜design work within a game development team

The O*NET profile for this occupation emphasizes office and team collaboration, design documents, and test iteration. Location, scheduling, tools, and project stage are confirmed with the employer, and US survey responses are not taken as uniform Chinese working conditions.
Organization and location｜a game development or related production team; actual office and remote arrangements are checked separately.
Materials and tools｜rule documents, configuration tables, flow, prototypes, tasks, and test feedback.
The design scope and the division with programming, art, testing, and production are confirmed by the specific team.
Scheduling and intensity｜iteration and release phases may involve time pressure, and specific shifts and hours are checked separately.
Discuss experience goals and implementation constraints and confirm whether feedback is a defect, a change, or a new hypothesis.
Review and responsibility｜Check the goal, rule consistency, implementable conditions, and test results.
Quality requirements｜Others can reproduce the rules and understand the changes, and personal experience is not presented as a general conclusion.

O*NET15-1255.01 provides core mechanics, documentation, prototyping, testing, and collaboration tasks.
The BLS15-1255 statistics cover web and digital interface designers and do not list this occupation separately.
The original notices from Tuyou, Changyou, and Tencent support their respective planner directions and submission conditions and do not represent all positions.

The GDC and Google/Harris surveys support discussion of AI in the game industry; the samples differ and are not treated as a national adoption rate for this occupation.

Video game designers design game goals, rules, mechanics, levels, story, and character background, write and maintain design documents, and work with programming, art, and testing teams to validate and iterate on gameplay. Liking games is only a starting point; explaining choices, breaking down rules, and accepting feedback matter more.
Researches search user intent and improves content visibility and marketing performance.
Researches computational theory and hardware and software problems and produces research plans and results.
Creates, modifies, and tests code and scripts, turning specifications into software behavior.
Develops websites and web applications, handling interaction, databases, and compatibility.
Systems and numbers gameplay design
Writes mechanic rules, configuration parameters, and balance tests.
A direction within this occupation focused on rule relationships and feedback loops, with the team division checked separately.
Willing to calculate states, check boundaries, and explain the reasons for changes.
Level and narrative design
Organizes level tasks, challenge, story, and character background.
A direction within this occupation emphasizing experience progression and collaborating with gameplay implementation.
Willing to design task flow and verify whether challenge and story connect.
Search marketing strategists
The output shifts to search marketing analysis and optimization, and gameplay design does not replace marketing evidence.
Willing to study user search, content, and marketing performance.
Computer and information research scientists
Moving into computational research requires research methods and the corresponding training, which game interest does not replace.
Willing to dig into theoretical problems and validate research methods.
Computer programmers
The output moves from design specifications to runnable code, requiring implementation and debugging evidence.
Willing to program, test, and locate defects over the long term.
Web developers
Moving into website implementation and operation requires browser, interface, and engineering ability.
Willing to build web applications and verify how they behave across devices and browsers.
Gameplay design directions and four adjacent occupations

First separate internal directions within this occupation from different occupations. Systems and numbers and level and narrative both center on game experience and implementation collaboration, while search marketing, computational research, programming, and web development have their own tasks and deliverables. Working on the same digital product does not mean duties can be swapped directly.

If you like writing rules, finding counterexamples, and tuning parameters, try systems and numbers first; if you like organizing challenge and story progression, try level and narrative first. When moving to another occupation, prove your ability with that occupation's research, marketing, or implementation output and check the specific job conditions.

This occupation and the four adjacent occupations use separate O*NET profiles: 15-1255.01, 13-1161.01, 15-1221.00, 15-1251.00, and 15-1254.00. The suitability signals and experience order are editorial suggestions, not official hiring standards.
After choosing a direction, analyze which tasks AI can assist with and how rule correctness, experience validation, and delivery responsibility are preserved.

Editorial suggestion: AI can draft mechanic alternatives or design explanations, but designers still check the goal, rules, and implementable conditions. Text generation is not gameplay validation and does not show that players will necessarily like it.

Task assistance, real adoption, and job outcomes are kept separate. Document drafts, test ideas, and prototype suggestions may need different validation; the uses below are editorial suggestions, not proof that a tool has improved efficiency in this occupation.

The GDC2026 official summary covers more than 2300 industry professionals; the Google/Harris2025 questionnaire covers 615 adult game developers in five countries. The samples and questions differ and are not merged into a national adoption rate for this occupation in China.

Editorial control suggestion: define the assisted task, the permitted data, and the reviewer. G20 uses only the fictional rules on this page to check states, costs, and failure tests; real internal design and player data are handled under team permission.

The BLS parent statistics for web and digital interface designers are used only to explain coverage limits and do not measure game design tool effects; neither occupational background nor wages can prove that AI has improved gameplay quality.

The generic NIST framework requires evaluating reliability by purpose and context. Citing the framework cannot be treated as proof that a specific game tool works, and an AI draft cannot replace design review and testing responsibility.

Designers must check the rule version, state changes, and boundary cases. G20 can calculate that a revised route is shorter and cannot thereby announce that players prefer it or that commercial revenue will rise.

Insufficient evidence: no attributable net AI job change for this occupation was obtained. A parent EMP total projection, industry layoff reporting, or a self-reported usage survey cannot directly imply a replacement headcount for this occupation.

NIST AI RMF1.0 provides ideas for context, purpose, and reliability evaluation. This page uses it to offer editorial testing suggestions; a framework is not an adoption rate or an effectiveness experiment for game designer tools.

If AI writes the rules, is that sufficient to confirm they are correct?
No. Check the initial state, costs, door and key conditions, and post-failure states step by step against G20; generated text may still omit limits.
Does the NIST framework prove a tool is effective?
No. The framework provides methods for limiting purpose and evaluating reliability, and the specific inputs, errors, and review costs need real testing.
How do you explore design assistance?

Use only the G20 fictional rules to ask a tool for test points and then verify them yourself against the original rules; keep the omissions and errors and do not use real internal design or player data.
Will AI automatically take on design review?
How many game design jobs will be reduced?
Insufficient evidence: no attributable net job change for this occupation was obtained. A parent projection and industry questionnaires cannot answer the causal replacement count for this occupation.
Can parent wages show tool efficiency gains in China?
No. Occupational wages do not measure tool effects, and the parent is not this occupation; Chinese actual work and evaluation conditions need independent evidence.
Can the usage percentages from the two surveys be averaged?

No. GDC covers many kinds of industry professionals, while Google/Harris covered 615 game developers in five countries without weighting; the sample periods and questions differ, and neither is a national rate for this occupation.

Being willing to write gameplay goals as explicit states and rules and then look for counterexamples is an exploration signal. One correct exercise is not enough to prove full job ability.

Liking games and being willing to design are different. When feedback arrives, first confirm the goal, rule version, and specific problem, then revise the specification and tests and explain the impact; G20 makes the door need no key, so both routes and the end key must be recalculated. Observe whether you are willing to repeat this process rather than only seeking approval for an idea.

Faced with feedback, you can first confirm the problem and version and then revise the rules and tests. Different opinions can be discussed on the evidence, without denying yourself or defending the original idea in place of validation.

The following three-track stages are an editorial learning arrangement, not a job grade or a promotion guarantee. Systems and numbers, level and narrative, and prototype collaboration each have a presentable output.

values: E1｜G20 offline key-and-door rules R0

Paper only. The map has only four one-way edges: S to K, K to D, S to D, and D to G, and no other movement exists. The start is S, energy is 4, and keys are 0; reaching G is a win and the key need not be kept.

Each successful move costs 1 energy, and energy must be at least 1 before moving; reaching K for the first time gains 1 key. In R0, D to G still requires 1 key, and a success consumes the key. An illegal edge, insufficient energy, or a missing key all fail, with position, energy, and keys all unchanged. Task: write the step-by-step states for S to K to D to G; then test attempting D to G after S to D, and test the input D, energy 0, key 1 attempting D to G.
E2 to E3｜mechanic change and work

E2 case A rule R1: other rules are unchanged, only D to G needs no key and consumes no key, and still costs 1 energy. Starting again from S, compare the direct S to D to G route with S to K to D to G. Case B in E2 claims: the direct route is shorter, so all players prefer R1. Judge whether that can be inferred.

E3 states the original fictional rules on this page, with the state reasoning and change explanations completed by me; there are no real players, commercial projects, or third-party material. Submit the rule table, the three R0 test cases, the two R1 routes, and the unknown experience questions.
Reference answers｜states, routes, and unknowns

The R0 key-collecting route: K has energy 3 and key 1, D has energy 2 and key 1, G has energy 1 and key 0, so it wins. Going directly to D gives energy 3 and key 0, and attempting D to G fails for lack of a key, still D/3/0. The input D/0/1 fails for insufficient energy, still D/0/1.

In R1, the direct route reaches D/3/0 then G/2/0 and wins; the key-collecting route goes K/3/1 then D/2/1 then G/1/1 and wins. The direct route uses 1 fewer successful move and leaves 1 more energy; the old key-collecting route is still legal, but reaching G no longer consumes a key. Case B cannot infer universal preference: no real player experience evidence was given. E3 reference statement: the source is the original fictional G20 rules created for this page, R0/R1; I completed the state reasoning, boundary tests, and change impact explanation. The work is for personal career exploration only and is not published; there is no real player data, commercial project, or third-party material, and it does not prove position qualification, hiring, or commercial results.
Practice boundaries

Do only offline paper states and rules; do not log in, pay, or invite real players to test. Calculation can verify legality and steps and cannot evaluate all player preferences or commercial revenue. When other exploration is needed, define the task and time boundaries first.

description.text: Video game designers design game goals, rules, mechanics, levels, story, and character background, write and maintain design documents, and work with programming, art, and testing teams to validate and iterate on gameplay. Liking games is only a starting point; explaining choices, breaking down rules, and accepting feedback matter more. No independent US wage and employment data were obtained, and parent web and digital interface designer statistics are not filled in; Chinese entry conditions are checked with the specific employer.
